metadata.proof: UploadHandler.post generates 6-character uploaded filenames using `random.choice()` (Python's Mersenne Twister PRNG, line 63-64) instead of `secrets.choice()`. extra.message: Unbounded File Upload Causes Memory/Disk Exhaustion

metadata.proof: Tornado buffers the entire multipart upload in memory when parsing self.request.files. The handler at line 60 receives the full file body, and line 67 writes the entire body blob to /tmp/ with no size check, chunking, or streaming. An attacker can upload a multi-gigabyte payload, exhausting server RAM (Tornado in-memory buffering) and filling the /tmp/ disk partition, causing a denial of service. This is distinct from CWE-434 (unrestricted file type) because it covers resource-exhaustion via unbounded file sizes, not missing validation of file content.

extra.message: Unbounded File Read in ContentHandler Exhausts Memory

metadata.proof: User-controlled input from the 'file' query parameter (line 75) is used to open a file at line 77. Line 78 calls read() with no argument, reading the entire file into memory with no size limit. Combined with the path traversal (CWE-22), an attacker can point to /dev/zero (which never returns EOF on read() under Python 2, causing indefinite memory growth until OOM) or a very large system log file (e.g., /var/log/system.log), exhausting server memory and causing denial of service. The existing CWE-22 covers directory traversal alone; it does not address the unbounded read that enables memory exhaustion.

extra.message: Unbounded File Upload — No Size Limit or Rate Limiting Enables Disk-Exhaustion DoS

metadata.proof: UploadHandler.post (lines 57-68) accepts multipart file uploads at POST /upload with zero constraints: no Content-Length pre-check, no file-size cap, no per-IP or global rate throttle. The handler writes file1['body'] directly to /tmp/ (line 67). An attacker can POST a single multi-gigabyte payload or flood the endpoint with thousands of concurrent uploads, exhausting the /tmp filesystem and causing a denial-of-service. No existing finding addresses the absence of resource allocation limits (CWE-770) on the upload handler.
